title: Effective script origin aliasing setup doesn't seem to match reality

labels.name: compat
labels.description: Standard is not web compatible or proprietary feature needs standardizing

body:
The way the HTML spec defines effective script origin aliasing is like so:

> An origin or effective script origin can be defined as an alias to another origin or effective script origin. The value of the origin or effective script origin is then the value of the origin or effective script origin to which it is an alias.

and it talks about how an origin or effective script origin can have three exclusive states: opaque identifier, tuple, alias.

The `document.domain` setter at https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#dom-document-domain step 8 says:

> If the effective script origin of this Document is an alias, set it to the value of the effective script origin (essentially de-aliasing the effective script origin).

OK, so what does this mean in practice?  Say we have a document that has an about:blank iframe.  The effective script origin of that iframe's document is an alias for the origin of the parent document.  If the parent sets document.domain, then they remain same-effective-script-origin.  But if the _child_ does, the spec says that it stops aliasing and they stop being same-effective-script-origin, because now the parent has whatever effective script origin it had, with whatever port it had, but the child has one with a "manual override" port.

This does not seem to be what browsers actually do.  An example testcase is at http://software.hixie.ch/utilities/js/live-dom-viewer/?saved=3951 and works as follows:
1. Create an iframe whose effective script origin is an alias
2. In the iframe, set a timeout with a string that attempts to get the `.frameElement` of the window.
3. Set `document.domain = document.domain` in the iframe.

The exact text of the testcase, just in case the live DOM viewer ever goes away:

```
<!DOCTYPE html>
<iframe id="x"></iframe>
<script>
onload = function() {
  var i = document.querySelector("#x");
  var win = i.contentWindow;
  win.w = w;
  win.frameEl = i;
  win.setTimeout("w(frameElement === frameEl)", 200);
  win.document.domain = win.document.domain;
}
</script>
```

Per spec as currently written, step 3 should de-alias and make the two windows not be the same effective script origin.  Then when the timeout fires the entry settings object is the iframe, and per https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsers.html#dom-frameelement step 5 null should be returned from the `.frameElement` getter.  That's not what I observe in at least Safari, Firefox, Chrome, IE11.  Edge13 is doing something weird in that id _does_ make the two windows different-effective-script-origin in this case, afaict, but then it has frameElement produce undefined or something.  Of course Edge13 also makes setting `document.domain` in the _parent_ de-alias afaict.  It's hard to tell....

In terms of actual implementation details, what Gecko does here is that there is an object representing the origin of the document.  This object can have two states: opaque identifier and tuple.  Aliasing is done by having both documents point to the same object.  This means that in my testcase above setting `document.domain` is symmetric across parent and child: both change the effective script origin of both documents.

This does mean that if you create a blob: or about:blank or javascript: or srcdoc document that's aliasing your origin it can also change your effective script origin if it tries to change its own, of course.  Maybe that's what the HTML Spec is trying to avoid?

Back to implementation details, I looked at Blink and they seem to do something similar.  Certainly their `document.domain` setter just modified, in-place, an object that the document has a pointer to.  And in the aliasing case they just have multiple documents point to the same object.  So the same setup as Gecko.  WebKit has the same setup as well (not surprising there).
